title: News Feed (Facebook / Instagram style)
problem: Design a news feed system that shows a user the latest posts from people they follow.
summary: A news feed system for ~300M DAU split into two halves the book defines explicitly: (1) feed publishing — a post service + fanout service that writes a new post and populates follower news-feed caches — and (2) news feed building — a news feed service that reads the precomputed cache and hydrates posts. The core tradeoff the book walks through is fan-out-on-write vs fan-out-on-read: pure on-write breaks on celebrity posts (a 100M-follower post = 100M writes), while pure on-read makes feed GET require N fan-ins of all followees' posts. The recommended solution is a hybrid — fan-out-on-write for regular users (precomputed timelines in Redis) and fan-out-on-read for celebrities with >1M followers, merged at read time for that small set. Backed by user/post/graph stores with aggressive caching (news feed cache, post cache, user cache), and a notification service that can ping followers about new content.

functional: Create a post with text and optional media
View a paginated feed of posts from followed users, newest first
Follow and unfollow users with immediate effect on the feed
Cursor-based pagination stable across new posts arriving
Notify followers (optional) when a followed user posts
nonFunctional: P99 feed read latency under 200 ms at 100K QPS peak
Post write visible to most followers within 5 seconds
99.95% availability for the feed read path
Cache hit ratio > 95% on timeline and post caches

assumptions: Average user opens feed 10x/day (3B feed reads/day)
1% of users are 'celebrities' (>1M followers) producing 20% of posts
Feed page = 20 posts; retained post window = 2 weeks
estimates: Fan-out writes (regular users only): 6K QPS * 200 avg followers ≈ 1.2M fanout writes/sec
Timeline cache size: 300M users * 20 post ids * 24B ≈ 150 GB in Redis

architecture.mermaid: graph LR client[Client] --> lb[Load Balancer] lb --> feedapi[News Feed Service] lb --> postsvc[Post Service] postsvc --> postdb[(Post / User / Graph DB)] postsvc --> fanoutq[Fanout Queue] postsvc --> notif[Notification Service] fanoutq --> fanout[Fanout Service] fanout --> graph[User Graph Service] fanout --> timeline[(News Feed Cache)] feedapi --> timeline feedapi --> postdb feedapi --> postcache[(Post + User Cache)]

client.name: Client (iOS / Android / Web)
client.summary: Mobile/web client that posts and pulls feed pages.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- POST /posts (text + media refs)
- GET /feed?cursor=... with pagination
- Optimistic UI: prepend new post locally before server ack

sections.heading: Offline behavior
sections.body: Queues drafts to local SQLite; retries with idempotency key on reconnect.

sections.heading: Why this matters for beginners
sections.body: Clients hide latency via optimistic rendering and prefetch — the backend can be slow on writes as long as the read path feels instant.

bottlenecks.title: Feed hydration payload bloat on cold scroll
bottlenecks.trigger: Each feed page = 20 posts with bodies + media_refs + author info. A user opening feed 10x/day and scrolling 3–5 pages pulls 60–100 posts; on cellular this can exceed 2–5 MB per session if media thumbnails aren't lazy-loaded.
bottlenecks.symptom: Slow first paint (>2s) on 3G/4G, users see spinners above the fold, higher app abandonment and increased feed-open-to-first-post latency in RUM.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Return minimal post skeleton (id, author_id, created_at, text, media_ref) in /feed; lazy-fetch media via CDN with responsive srcset; use HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 multiplexing; prefetch next page only when user is within 5 posts of the end.
bottlenecks.detection: Client RUM metric: p95 time-to-first-post < 800ms; alert if feed payload size p95 > 500KB or if first-page render > 1.5s on cellular.

bottlenecks.title: Optimistic post reconciliation drift on flaky networks
bottlenecks.trigger: Client prepends post locally before server ack; if the POST /posts retry loop (idempotency-key based) takes >10s or the network flaps mid-flight, duplicate UI entries or ghost posts can appear. At 300M DAU posting 2x/day, even a 0.05% reconciliation bug = 300K bad UX events/day.
bottlenecks.symptom: Users see duplicate posts in their own composer feed, or posts stuck with a 'sending...' state that never clears; support tickets about 'I posted twice'.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Strict client-side state machine: {draft → pending(idemp_key) → confirmed(server_post_id) | failed}; dedupe on idempotency-key before rendering; cap retries at 5 with exponential backoff; persist pending queue in SQLite with WAL so crashes don't lose state.
bottlenecks.detection: Log client-side metric `post_reconcile_duration_ms` and `duplicate_post_detected_count`; alert if duplicates > 0.01% of posts or if pending→confirmed p99 > 30s.

bottlenecks.title: Offline draft queue unbounded growth
bottlenecks.trigger: Client queues drafts to local SQLite when offline. A user offline for days (flights, travel) who composes many posts — or a bug that fails to drain the queue on reconnect — can grow the SQLite DB to hundreds of MB, especially with media references attached.
bottlenecks.symptom: App storage bloat, slow app startup (SQLite open + migration scan), eventually iOS/Android kills the app or the OS shows 'storage full'; on reconnect a thundering herd of retries hits POST /posts.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cap offline draft queue at 50 entries with FIFO eviction warning UI; throttle reconnect drain to 1 post/sec with jitter; vacuum SQLite weekly; store media on disk (not BLOB in SQLite) and reference by path.
bottlenecks.detection: Client telemetry: `draft_queue_size` histogram and `app_local_storage_mb`; alert if p99 queue depth > 20 or storage > 100MB for the app sandbox.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the client is called out as a design component In most system designs the client feels like "just the app" — but for a news feed serving 300M DAU with 35K peak feed reads/sec, the client is actively doing work to hide backend latency. It renders optimistically (the post you just composed appears *before* the server acknowledges it), paginates with cursors so the News Feed Service only has to return 20 posts at a time, and lazy-loads media through the CDN so the initial feed payload stays small. Without those behaviors, the whole hybrid fanout design behind it would still feel slow. ## What happens if the client is "dumb" Imagine the client just blocks on `POST /posts` and waits for fanout to finish before showing the new post. The Post Service returns 201 in ~20–40ms, but fanout to 200 followers is async and can take 1–5s. The user sees a spinner, taps again, and now the Post Service is deduping on idempotency key to avoid double-posts — extra load on Redis, extra support tickets about "did my post go through?". Same story on reads: without cursor pagination, a scroll would refetch the whole feed and hammer the Timeline Cache. ## The number that makes this matter Feed reads peak at **100K QPS** (300M DAU × 10 opens/day ÷ 86400). If each feed open pulled full post bodies plus media instead of a lazy-loaded skeleton — say 2MB vs 200KB — that's 200 GB/sec of egress vs 20 GB/sec. The client's lazy-loading is what keeps the CDN bill and mobile data usage sane. ## Trade-off The designer accepted more client-side complexity (optimistic state machines, offline SQLite queues, reconciliation bugs) in exchange for a feed that feels instant even when the backend is doing async work behind the scenes.

lb.name: Load Balancer
lb.summary: L7 LB with sticky routing by user id for cache locality.

sections.heading: Algorithm
sections.body: Consistent hash on user id → improves timeline-cache shard locality when the feed API uses a shard-aware client.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Single LB replica failure → failover to standby within 1–2s.
- Whole-zone outage → DNS/anycast shifts to healthy zone.

bottlenecks.title: Consistent-hash hot shard from celebrity-following users
bottlenecks.trigger: Consistent-hash on user_id routes ~100K peak feed QPS across feed API replicas, but traffic isn't uniform — users following the same celebrity (e.g., author 101 with 80M followers) all issue merge-on-read ZREVRANGE for `celeb-posts:101`, and whichever feed replicas own those users can see 2–5x the baseline QPS of ~3K/replica across 35 replicas.
bottlenecks.symptom: A subset of feed API replicas saturate CPU/connection pools while peers sit at 30% utilization; p99 feed latency on those replicas climbs from ~30ms to >500ms; LB's per-upstream active-connection metric shows skewed fan-in.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Switch LB to 'bounded-load consistent hashing' (Envoy's `maglev` with `hash_balance_factor: 1.25`) so overloaded upstreams overflow to the next replica; or fall back to least-request when an upstream exceeds 1.5x mean load.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-upstream `envoy_cluster_upstream_rq_active` variance; alert if max/median replica QPS ratio > 2.0 over a 1-min window, or if any single upstream exceeds 5K concurrent requests.

bottlenecks.title: TLS handshake CPU exhaustion at 100K peak feed QPS
bottlenecks.trigger: 100K peak feed reads/sec + 20K peak post writes/sec = 120K QPS at the LB. Mobile clients on flaky cellular reconnect often; if session-resumption hit rate drops below ~90%, full TLS handshakes (ECDHE + cert verify) cost ~1–2ms of CPU each, and 12K new handshakes/sec can saturate a single LB instance's CPU before connection limits kick in.
bottlenecks.symptom: LB CPU pegged at 100% while request throughput plateaus well under the declared 50K concurrency; clients see TLS timeouts or connection resets; feed-open p95 spikes to multi-second on app cold start.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable TLS 1.3 with 0-RTT resumption, offload to dedicated NICs with TLS-in-hardware (AWS NLB+ACM or Envoy with BoringSSL ASM), and pre-warm session tickets with a 24h rotation. Set `ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:100m` equivalents.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor `ssl_handshake_latency_ms` p99 and `ssl_session_reuse_ratio`; alert if reuse < 85% or handshake p99 > 10ms. Track LB CPU per core — alert at sustained >70%.

bottlenecks.title: Zone failover storm when consistent-hash ring reshuffles
bottlenecks.trigger: On a whole-zone LB outage, DNS/anycast shifts all 100K feed QPS to a healthy zone within 1–2s. The new zone's LB has a different consistent-hash ring membership, so ~1/3 of users rehash to different feed API replicas with cold shard-affinity caches — turning warm Redis client-side connection pools and local user metadata caches into misses.
bottlenecks.symptom: Immediately after failover, feed latency p95 jumps from 30ms to 200–400ms for several minutes; Redis `tl:{user}` access pattern shows a surge of cross-shard hops; timeline cache hit ratio drops temporarily.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a globally coordinated hash ring (shared ring state in etcd/Consul across zones) so failover preserves user→replica mapping; pre-warm standby LB with anticipated ring state; cap rehash blast radius with rendezvous hashing instead of naive mod-N.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `lb_upstream_rehash_rate` during zone events; alert if >20% of active sessions remap within 60s. Correlate with feed API `cache_miss_ratio` — alert if it doubles within 2min of an LB topology change.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a load balancer sits in front of the news feed The news feed has two very different traffic shapes hitting the same public endpoint: ~20K peak post writes/sec going to the Post Service and ~100K peak feed reads/sec going to the News Feed Service. No single server can handle that, so we run ~35 feed replicas and a pool of post replicas. Something has to decide which replica each request goes to — that's the load balancer's job. But it's doing more than round-robin: it hashes on `user_id` so the *same* user tends to land on the *same* feed replica, which keeps that replica's in-process caches (user metadata, celebrity-follow lists, Redis connection pools) warm for that user. ## What breaks without it If clients hit feed replicas directly (say via DNS round-robin), one replica crashing means a chunk of users get errors until DNS TTLs expire — minutes of partial outage. Worse, without user-affinity routing, every replica ends up being a cold cache for every user, so the Timeline Cache gets hammered with cross-shard lookups and p99 feed latency balloons from ~30ms into the hundreds. The operator sees uneven CPU across replicas and a mysterious Redis hotspot. ## The number that matters At 100K peak feed QPS across 35 replicas, that's ~2.9K QPS per replica *on average*. Without consistent-hash routing, you'd also pay a cache-miss penalty on nearly every request; with it, a returning user hits a replica that already knows them. ## Trade-off Sticky hashing can create hot shards when many users follow the same celebrity — which is why the design notes bounded-load consistent hashing as a mitigation.

feedapi.name: News Feed Service
feedapi.summary: The book's 'news feed service' (read side). Reads precomputed news-feed cache + merges celebrity posts at read time, then hydrates post bodies + author info from caches.

sections.heading: News feed building
sections.body: The book describes this service as the side of the system that fetches news feed. It resolves the user's ids-only timeline, hydrates post content via post cache + user cache, and returns the page to the client.

sections.heading: Read algorithm (hybrid)
sections.body:
1. `ZREVRANGE tl:{user} 0 19` → 20 post ids from precomputed news-feed cache
2. Fetch the user's celebrity follow list (small, cached)
3. For each celebrity, `ZREVRANGE celeb-posts:{id}` — merge by timestamp
4. Batch GET post bodies from post cache (fallback to DB)
5. Batch GET author display info from user cache
6. Return page + cursor

sections.heading: Why hybrid
sections.body:
The book explicitly enumerates the tradeoff:
- Fan-out-on-write: feed is instant (pre-computed) but write amplifies by followers — 100M-follower post = 100M writes. Inactive users still have their feed updated, which is wasted work.
- Fan-out-on-read: no write amplification but every feed request requires N fan-ins across followees, which is slow and hammers hot author partitions.
- Hybrid: fan-out-on-write for everyone below 1M followers, merge-on-read only for the tiny celebrity set. Caps write amplification and keeps p99 feed latency low.

sections.heading: Scaling
sections.body: 35K QPS peak, ~10ms service time → ~350 concurrent in-flight → ~35 replicas at 1000 concurrency each.

gained: Single round trip for post + author + counts
lost: Harder to cache responses at edge

bottlenecks.title: Celebrity fan-in amplification on every feed read
bottlenecks.trigger: At 100K peak feed QPS, each read issues 1 ZREVRANGE on tl:{user} plus one ZREVRANGE per followed celebrity. If average user follows 2-5 celebrities, that's 300K-600K Redis ops/sec just for celeb-posts merges. A power user following 50 celebrities (A-list accounts) turns one feed open into 51 Redis round-trips, pushing p99 from ~30ms to 200ms+.
bottlenecks.symptom: Feed p99 latency climbs non-linearly with celebrities-followed; Redis CPU on celeb-posts shards saturates; hot celeb-posts:{id} keys (e.g., a Kardashian) show per-key QPS in the tens of thousands on a single shard.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Pipeline all celeb ZREVRANGE calls in one Redis MULTI; cap per-user celeb-merge set to top-20 most-recently-active celebs and lazy-load the rest on scroll; add a 30s edge cache per celeb-posts:{id} key (since all viewers see the same celeb feed) to collapse thundering reads into one backend call.
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram `feed_celeb_fanin_count` per request and `feed_latency_ms` bucketed by celeb-count; alert when p99 latency for users with >10 celebs-followed exceeds 150ms, or when any single celeb-posts:{id} key exceeds 5K QPS on a Redis shard.

bottlenecks.title: Timeline cache miss storm on inactive-user return
bottlenecks.trigger: Timeline cache uses allkeys-LRU on a 150GB working set. Inactive users (weeks away) get evicted. When they return — think Monday-morning commute spike or a viral event pulling lapsed users back — 35K QPS can include 10-20% cold users, each requiring on-read rebuild by scanning followees' posts. That's potentially 3-7K rebuild ops/sec, each fan-in-ing 200 followees.
bottlenecks.symptom: Feed service thread pools (3000 concurrency) saturate; p95 latency jumps from ~30ms to several seconds for cold users; cascading pressure on Post Store (Cassandra) from millions of SELECT BY author_id scans; Kafka fanout topic may be replayed to rebuild, adding more latency.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a second cache tier (Aerospike or Redis-on-flash) for warm-but-not-hot timelines at $/GB, raising effective cache depth from 20 posts to 200; on miss, return a degraded 'recent posts from top-10 followees' response in <200ms via a bounded fan-in (not all 200 followees); pre-warm timelines for users with login-prediction signals (push notification opened).
bottlenecks.detection: Track `timeline_cache_hit_ratio` per feed request; alert if it drops below 95%. Monitor `feed_cold_rebuild_duration_ms` p99 and `feed_cold_rebuild_qps` — alert if rebuilds exceed 2K/sec sustained.

bottlenecks.title: Post+user cache MGET tail latency dominating feed p99
bottlenecks.trigger: Each feed page hydrates 20 posts + ~14 distinct authors = 34 MGET keys, often spread across multiple Redis shards. At 100K feed QPS this is ~3.4M key lookups/sec. With even a 0.5% miss rate (post cache evictions past the 2-week window or cold authors), ~17K DB fallbacks/sec hit Post Store's 3-10ms service time — which becomes the tail of every feed response because the service must wait for all 20 posts before responding.
bottlenecks.symptom: Feed p99 sits at 80-150ms despite p50 at 15ms; flame graphs show time spent waiting on the slowest MGET shard or a single DB fallback; sporadic 'slow feed' complaints correlate with users whose feeds include older (evicted) posts.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use hash-tagged keys `p:{shard_id}:{post_id}` so batches of posts co-locate on one shard, reducing scatter-gather; issue DB fallbacks in parallel with a 20ms hedge timeout; return partial feed (skip the 1-2 missing posts, backfill on next page) rather than blocking; raise post cache TTL from 1h to 24h for posts <7 days old.
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram `feed_hydrate_mget_p99` and `feed_db_fallback_count_per_request`; alert if p99 MGET > 10ms or if >5% of feed requests require any DB fallback. Track per-shard Redis latency variance — alert when max/p50 shard latency ratio exceeds 3x.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the News Feed Service is here In this news feed design, posting and reading are two completely different workloads. Writing a post is rare (2/day per user) but reading the feed is constant (10/day per user). The News Feed Service exists because *reading* a feed isn't just "SELECT posts FROM db" — it's a multi-step dance: pull the precomputed list of post IDs from the Timeline Cache, merge in fresh posts from celebrities the user follows (the hybrid trick), then hydrate those IDs into real post bodies and author info from two more caches. Somebody has to orchestrate that, and it has to be a dedicated service because the read path is where almost all the traffic lives. ## What happens without it If the client tried to do this orchestration itself, every feed open would mean ~4 round trips over cellular before the first post renders — easily 500ms+ of added latency, and you'd expose your Redis clusters directly to mobile apps (a security and versioning nightmare). If you merged it into the Post Service instead, a spike in reads would starve post writes of CPU and connection pool slots; operators would see writes timing out during a viral moment precisely when users most want to post. ## The number that matters Feed reads peak at **100K QPS** (300M DAU × 10 opens/day ÷ 86400s), versus 20K QPS for post writes. That's a 5:1 read/write ratio — the read path deserves its own service, its own replica count (~35), and its own scaling curve. At ~10ms service time, 100K QPS × 0.01s = 1000 concurrent requests in flight, comfortably spread across those 35 replicas. ## Trade-off Splitting read from write adds a service to operate, but it lets each side scale and fail independently.

postsvc.name: Post Service (Feed Publishing)
postsvc.summary: The book's 'feed publishing' entry point. Handles post creation, validation, stores the post, and kicks off fanout + notification.

sections.heading: Feed publishing responsibilities
sections.body:
- Validate + store post in Post Store (source of truth)
- Enqueue a fanout event so the fanout service can populate followers' news-feed caches
- Emit a notification event for the notification service
- Return 201 + post_id immediately — fanout is async

sections.heading: Celebrity cutoff
sections.body: If `author.follower_count > 1_000_000`, skip fanout entirely — the news feed service will merge the celebrity's posts on read. This is the 'hybrid' optimization.

sections.heading: Idempotency
sections.body: Client sends `Idempotency-Key`; Post Service dedupes within a 24h window via a Redis SET.

bottlenecks.title: Idempotency-key Redis SET unbounded growth + hot key contention
bottlenecks.trigger: At 7K sustained / 20K peak post writes/sec with a 24h dedup window, the idempotency store accumulates ~600M entries/day. Using `SISMEMBER/SADD` on a per-user key like `idemp:{user_id}` turns heavy posters (celebrities, bots, scheduled publishers) into hot keys — a single Redis shard sees thousands of ops/sec for one member while the set grows unbounded over the 24h window.
bottlenecks.symptom: Post write p99 climbs from ~20ms to 100ms+; Redis CPU saturation on a small number of shards; occasional `MOVED` storms during resharding; duplicate posts slip through when Redis evicts the idempotency set under memory pressure (allkeys-lru).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use per-key entries with TTL instead of per-user sets: `SET idemp:{user}:{key} {post_id} EX 86400 NX` — O(1), auto-expiring, evenly distributed via hash slot. Size Redis cluster for ~600M keys × ~80B ≈ 50GB with `volatile-ttl` eviction; add a Bloom filter in-process as a pre-check to cut Redis RTT on the 99.9% non-duplicate path.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Redis per-shard QPS variance (max/median > 3x), idempotency Redis memory > 70%, and a business metric `duplicate_post_detected_rate` > 0.01%; track `idemp_check_latency_ms` p99 with alert at 5ms.

bottlenecks.title: Dual-write inconsistency between Post Store and Kafka fanout topic
bottlenecks.trigger: Post service writes to Cassandra (`LOCAL_QUORUM`, 3–10ms) AND produces to Kafka `feed.fanout` before returning 201. At 20K peak writes/sec, even a 0.1% Kafka produce failure after a successful DB commit = 20 posts/sec that exist in Post Store but never fan out — invisible posts for 150 followers each = 3K broken feeds/sec.
bottlenecks.symptom: Users report 'I posted but my friends can't see it'; support tickets correlate with Kafka broker incidents or network blips; post exists via direct URL (GET /posts/{id}) but never appears in any follower's feed even after hours.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Adopt the transactional outbox pattern: in the same Cassandra batch (or via a lightweight MySQL outbox table), write the post row AND an `outbox_events` row; a Debezium/CDC consumer drains the outbox to Kafka with at-least-once delivery. Alternatively, produce to Kafka FIRST with the snowflake id, then write to DB, and have a reconciler fix gaps. Never return 201 until both legs are durable.
bottlenecks.detection: Emit a `post_created` counter at DB-commit and a `fanout_enqueued` counter at Kafka-ack; alert if the ratio drifts > 0.05% over a 5-min window. Run an hourly reconciliation job that scans `posts` created in the last hour and checks fanout topic offsets; page on any gap.

bottlenecks.title: Celebrity follower_count lookup blocking the write path
bottlenecks.trigger: Post service must know `author.follower_count` to decide the hybrid cutoff (>1M = skip fanout). If this requires a User Graph Service call on every write, that's 20K peak QPS of synchronous graph reads adding 5–15ms + 0.05% failure rate per call. For a celebrity posting burst (award shows, news events), the same hot author_id hammers one graph shard.
bottlenecks.symptom: Post write p95 latency is dominated by graph-service tail latency rather than DB+Kafka; graph service becomes a hard dependency for posting — a graph outage means nobody can post at all, not just nobody can see follower lists.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cache `follower_count` denormalized on the user record in the user cache (`u:{user_id}`) with 60s TTL; update it asynchronously via a follow-event consumer. For the celebrity decision specifically, maintain a small in-memory bloom/set of known-celebrity user_ids (~1% of 300M = 3M ids, ~4MB with a compact encoding) refreshed every 5 min — eliminates the sync call entirely on the write path.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `post_write_graph_call_latency_ms` p99 (alert >20ms) and `celebrity_decision_source` counter (cache-hit vs graph-fallback); alert if graph-fallback rate > 1% of writes. Monitor post service error rate correlation with graph service availability.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Post Service is here In this news feed design, writing a post kicks off a chain reaction: the post has to be stored durably, ~150 follower timelines need to be updated, and a notification might go out. The Post Service exists to be the single entry point that owns that orchestration — it validates the post, assigns a snowflake ID, writes to the Post Store, and then hands off asynchronously to fanout and notifications via Kafka. Crucially, it's also where the **celebrity cutoff** decision lives: if the author has >1M followers, skip fanout entirely and let reads merge them in. Without a dedicated service making that call, the hybrid fan-out model the book recommends has nowhere to live. ## What breaks without it If the client wrote directly to Cassandra and Kafka, every mobile app version would need to know the celebrity threshold, the idempotency rules, and the Kafka topic schema — and a bad client release could double-post or skip fanout entirely. Operators would see duplicate posts in user feeds, mismatched follower_count decisions, and no single place to add rate limits when a spam wave hits. Worse, you'd expose Cassandra and Kafka credentials to untrusted clients. ## The number that matters Post writes run at **7K QPS sustained, 20K peak** (300M DAU × 2 posts/day ÷ 86400s). The Post Service returns 201 in ~20–40ms by making fanout *async* — if it waited for fanout to 150 followers (1–5s), a single replica at 2000 concurrency could only sustain ~400 QPS instead of 10K+. ## Trade-off Async fanout means a follower might not see the post for 1–5 seconds after the author sees "Posted ✓" — eventual consistency on the read side in exchange for a fast, decoupled write path.

postdb.name: Post Store
postdb.summary: Source-of-truth post content, keyed by post_id.

sections.heading: Data model
sections.body:
```
TABLE posts post_id BIGINT PK (snowflake) author_id BIGINT created_at TIMESTAMP body TEXT media_refs LIST<TEXT>
```

sections.heading: Why Cassandra
sections.body: Heavy write QPS (7K sustained, 20K peak), PK lookup only, multi-DC replication for user proximity. MySQL sharded by `hash(post_id)` works too.

sections.heading: Retention
sections.body: 2-week hot window on SSD; older posts cold-tiered to S3 + Glacier for cheap storage.

gained: Tight Hadoop integration for offline analytics

bottlenecks.title: Cache-miss read storm from feed hydration overwhelming Cassandra
bottlenecks.trigger: Feed reads peak at 100K QPS, each hydrating ~20 posts (2M potential post lookups/sec). Post cache normally absorbs these, but a cache cold-start (Redis failover, deploy, eviction of 2-week window boundary) or a 1% miss rate pushes 20K QPS of MGET-fallback SELECT-by-post_id straight onto Post Store — 10x normal write load of 7K QPS.
bottlenecks.symptom: Cassandra read latency p99 jumps from 10ms to 100ms+, coordinator nodes saturate CPU, news feed service thread pools block on DB reads, feed p95 climbs from ~30ms to several seconds, cascading timeouts.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Provision Cassandra read capacity for 3-5x steady-state (at least 30K QPS headroom); use request hedging with a 20ms timeout so one slow replica doesn't dominate; enable row cache for posts <24h old; implement negative caching for tombstoned posts; rate-limit fallback reads per feed replica with a circuit breaker that returns partial feeds.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `cassandra_read_qps` > 15K sustained for 1 min, `post_cache_miss_ratio` > 2%, or `post_db_read_latency_p99` > 25ms. Track correlation between Redis cluster events and Cassandra QPS spikes.

bottlenecks.title: Celebrity author hot partition on write + scan patterns
bottlenecks.trigger: Posts table is PK'd by post_id (good for lookups), but any secondary access by author_id (e.g., rebuild celeb-posts ZSET after Redis failure, profile timeline view, moderation scans) hits one author's rows. A celebrity with 80M followers posting during a viral event gets scanned by recovery jobs + profile views; if author_id is a secondary index or partition key in a denormalized table, one Cassandra node owns all their posts = 10s of MB per partition + hot-spot reads.
bottlenecks.symptom: One Cassandra node shows 5-10x CPU/disk I/O vs peers, `nodetool tpstats` shows pending ReadStage on that node, `SELECT... WHERE author_id=101` queries time out, compaction lag on the hot node, gossip flapping.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a composite partition key `(author_id, bucket)` where bucket = floor(created_at / 1day) to cap partition size; cache celeb-posts ZSET rebuild source in a dedicated denormalized table `posts_by_author_bucketed`; avoid ALLOW FILTERING scans on posts table; run compaction with TWCS (time-window compaction strategy) given the 2-week hot window.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor per-node `cassandra_cpu_utilization` variance (max/median > 2x), partition size histogram (alert at p99 > 100MB), `pending_read_stage` > 50 on any node, and compaction backlog > 10GB on a single node.

bottlenecks.title: Cold-tier retrieval latency when users scroll past 2-week hot window
bottlenecks.trigger: Retention policy keeps 2 weeks on SSD; older posts are cold-tiered to S3+Glacier. Users scrolling deep history (profile views, bookmarks, shared links to old posts) or replay operations hit cold storage. S3 Standard reads are 50-200ms; Glacier is minutes-to-hours. At even 0.1% of 100K feed QPS touching old posts = 100 QPS of high-latency reads blocking hydration.
bottlenecks.symptom: Sporadic feed p99 spikes to seconds, users report old shared links load slowly or fail, profile 'see older posts' pagination stalls, hydration batch requests have one slow post blocking the whole batch response.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tier cold posts to S3 Standard (not Glacier) for the first 90 days since access is latency-sensitive; only Glacier after 90d; pre-warm cold posts into post cache asynchronously on first miss; return a placeholder 'post archived — loading' skeleton to client rather than blocking the feed page; use hedged reads across S3 regions.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `post_cold_tier_fetch_latency_ms` p99 (alert > 500ms), `post_cold_tier_fetch_qps` (alert if > 200 sustained), and `feed_request_blocked_by_cold_fetch_ratio` (alert > 0.5% of feed requests).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Post Store is here Everything else in this design is a *cache* or a *derived index*. The Timeline Cache holds post IDs, not post bodies. The Post+User Cache holds bodies but evicts under memory pressure. Kafka retains fanout events for 7 days and then drops them. If every one of those layers lost its data tomorrow, the Post Store is what lets us rebuild — it's the durable source of truth for the actual content a user wrote. For a news feed serving 300M DAU, you cannot put post bodies *only* in Redis; a Redis failover would mean permanently deleted posts, which is a product-ending bug. ## What breaks without it Imagine the News Feed Service reads 20 post IDs from the Timeline Cache, then tries to hydrate them — but the Post+User Cache evicted anything older than its LRU window. With no backing store, those IDs are now dangling references: the user sees "Post unavailable" gaps in their feed. Worse, when Redis is rebooted or a shard is lost, every post ever written is gone. Operators would see feed hydration miss rates climb toward 100% and have no way to recover. ## The number that matters At 7K sustained post writes/sec (20K peak) × 86,400s/day ≈ **600M new posts/day**. Cassandra is chosen because writes are the hot path here — PK lookup by `post_id` is exactly one partition, and LOCAL_QUORUM gives durability across 3 replicas without the coordination overhead a relational DB would impose at this write rate. ## Trade-off Cassandra gives up rich queries (no "posts where body contains X") in exchange for predictable write throughput and easy multi-DC replication.

fanoutq.name: Fanout Queue (Kafka)
fanoutq.summary: Durable log of fanout jobs to decouple post write from timeline writes.

sections.heading: Partitioning
sections.body: Partition key = `author_id` so all events for one author land in order on the same partition. 200 partitions comfortably handle 20K peak events/sec.

sections.heading: Delivery semantics
sections.body: At-least-once; fanout worker is idempotent on `(user_id, post_id)` so duplicate delivery is harmless.

sections.heading: Why Kafka
sections.body: Retention (7 days) lets us replay fanouts if a downstream outage loses timeline writes. SQS would require a separate dead-letter strategy.

lost: No strict ordering without FIFO (with throughput cap)

bottlenecks.title: Partition hot-spotting from high-follower (near-celebrity) authors
bottlenecks.trigger: Partition key is author_id across 200 partitions for 20K peak events/sec (~100 events/sec/partition average). But authors just under the 1M-follower celebrity cutoff (e.g., 500K–999K followers) still go through fan-out-on-write and their events carry the heaviest downstream work. A popular author posting a burst lands all events on one partition, and with `author_id` keying, each large author's traffic pins to a single partition/broker.
bottlenecks.symptom: Consumer lag alarm fires on 1–2 partitions while the other 198 are at zero lag; one broker shows 5–10x CPU/network vs peers; fanout-to-timeline SLO (1–5s follower visibility) breaches for followers of large authors while regular users are fine; ISR shrinks on the hot partition.
bottlenecks.mitigation: For authors with >100K followers, switch the producer key to `author_id:shard` where shard = hash(post_id) % N (N=8–16), trading strict per-author ordering for load spread — fanout workers are already idempotent on (follower_id, post_id) so ordering doesn't matter. Also rebalance partitions with a custom partitioner that weights by recent author follower_count, and raise partition count from 200 to 500 to give the rebalancer more room.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on per-partition lag variance: `max(kafka_consumergroup_lag) / p50(kafka_consumergroup_lag) > 5` sustained 2 min; per-broker `BytesInPerSec` max/median > 3x; track producer-side `record-send-rate` histogram by partition.

bottlenecks.title: Consumer lag explosion during celebrity-adjacent viral bursts
bottlenecks.trigger: Steady-state is 7K events/sec but fanout writes downstream are 1.2M ZADDs/sec (≈170x amplification). A viral moment (breaking news, sports final) can 3–5x post rate to 60K+ events/sec briefly. If fanout workers (100 workers × 12K ZADDs/sec) can't scale fast enough, Kafka absorbs the backlog — at 60K events/sec × avg 200 followers = 12M downstream writes/sec demand vs 1.2M capacity, so lag grows at ~50K events/sec.
bottlenecks.symptom: Kafka consumer-group lag on `feed.fanout` climbs past the 60s alert threshold; followers see post-to-feed-visibility latency go from ~2s to minutes; on-call sees disk usage on Kafka brokers climbing since 7-day retention means backed-up messages aren't evicted; fanout worker CPU is pinned at 100%.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Auto-scale fanout workers on Kafka lag metric (KEDA or custom HPA on `kafka_consumergroup_lag_sum`) with target lag < 30s; pre-provision 2x baseline worker capacity for predictable events (sports, elections); implement priority lanes — a second topic `feed.fanout.priority` for verified/high-engagement authors so background catchup doesn't starve fresh posts. Consider lowering the celebrity threshold from 1M to 500K during incidents to shed write amplification.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert at `kafka_consumergroup_lag > 60s` (existing SLI) with 2-min evaluation; predictive alert on `d(lag)/dt > 1000 msgs/sec` sustained 30s to catch growing backlogs before they breach; dashboard lag/worker-count/downstream-write-rate on one view.

bottlenecks.title: Broker throughput saturation on fanout event payload size
bottlenecks.trigger: At 20K peak events/sec, each fanout record carries post_id, author_id, follower_count, created_at, and possibly denormalized post metadata to avoid fanout-worker DB lookups. At ~500B per record that's 10 MB/sec ingress, but with 3x replication factor = 30 MB/sec replication traffic, plus consumers reading at full rate = another 10 MB/sec egress. A 7-day retention at 20K events/sec × 500B × 86400 × 7 ≈ 6 TB per cluster just for this topic.
bottlenecks.symptom: Broker disk utilization climbs steadily; `BytesInPerSec` + `BytesOutPerSec` + replication traffic saturates the broker NIC (1 Gbps ≈ 125 MB/sec theoretical, ~80 MB/sec practical); producer `request-latency-avg` creeps up from 2ms to 20ms+; ISR lag warnings on replica followers.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable producer-side compression (`compression.type=zstd`, typical 3–4x ratio brings events to ~125B → 2.5 MB/sec ingress); keep payloads minimal — only post_id, author_id, follower_count flag (let fanout worker fetch full post from Post Store cache); reduce retention on `feed.fanout` from 7d to 2d since replay beyond 2d is rarely useful (timeline cache rebuild from Post Store is preferred for older gaps); right-size brokers to 10 Gbps NICs if on-prem.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor `kafka_server_BrokerTopicMetrics_BytesInPerSec` and `ReplicationBytesInPerSec` per broker, alert at 60% of NIC capacity; track topic log size growth rate and alert if 7d projection exceeds 70% of disk; watch `request-latency-avg` on producer, alert > 10ms.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a Fanout Queue sits between posting and timeline updates When a user taps "Post," two very different things need to happen: the post must be saved durably (fast — one DB write), and ~150 follower timelines must be updated (slow — 150 Redis writes, sometimes thousands). If the Post Service tried to do both before returning 201, the user would stare at a spinner for 1–5 seconds every time they posted. The Fanout Queue is what lets the Post Service say "I've durably recorded your post, go" in ~20–40ms, and then let fanout workers grind through the follower updates in the background. Kafka specifically (vs. an in-memory queue) is chosen because its 7-day retention means if the fanout workers crash or a Redis shard goes down, we can **replay** events to rebuild missing timelines — the post isn't lost. ## What breaks without it If the Post Service called the Fanout Service directly (synchronously), a slow User Graph lookup or a Redis hiccup would block the post-write path. Users see "post failed" errors during exactly the moments when traffic is highest (viral events). Operators see post-write p99 latency spike and cascading timeouts chewing through Post Service threads. ## The number that matters Post writes peak at **20K QPS**, and each post fans out to ~200 followers on average → **1.2M downstream timeline writes/sec at peak**. Kafka absorbs that 60× amplification as a buffer: producers write 20K records/sec, and 100 fanout workers each drain ~12K ZADDs/sec downstream at their own pace. Without the buffer, a burst would slam Redis directly and drop writes. ## Trade-off The designer accepted eventual consistency (followers see the post 1–5s late) in exchange for fast, decoupled writes that survive downstream outages.

fanout.name: Fanout Service
fanout.summary: The book's 'fanout service' — reads fanout events, looks up followers, prepends post_id to each follower's news-feed cache (fan-out-on-write). For celebrities it skips the write entirely (fan-out-on-read).

sections.heading: Fan-out-on-write (default, book )
sections.body:
1. Consume `{post_id, author_id}`
2. `followers = user_graph.get_followers(author_id)` (paginated)
3. For each follower batch: `ZADD tl:{follower} {score=created_at} {post_id}`; `ZREMRANGEBYRANK tl:{follower} 0 -1001` (keep top 1000)
Book's key property: at feed read, the news-feed cache already has the answer — no fan-in required.

sections.heading: Fan-out-on-read (celebrities)
sections.body: If `followers > 1M`, do nothing here. At read time, the News Feed Service will fan-IN celebrity posts from `celeb-posts:{author}` and merge them with the viewer's precomputed timeline. Turns 100M writes into ~few reads.

sections.heading: Backpressure
sections.body: 1.2M fanout writes/sec peak → 100 workers * 12K ZADDs/sec each. Kafka consumer lag is the canonical SLI; alert at >60s lag.

sections.heading: Book's pros/cons of fanout-on-write
sections.body:
Pros: feed read is instant; works well for users with few friends.
Cons: slow for high-follower users (hotspot on write); storage wasted on inactive users' precomputed feeds.
This is why the book concludes with the hybrid approach.

gained: Stateful joins with user graph in-memory
lost: Heavier cluster to run than stateless workers

bottlenecks.title: User-graph pagination stalls fanout on high-follower (sub-celebrity) authors
bottlenecks.trigger: Authors with 100K–1M followers still take the fan-out-on-write path. At 5ms–15ms per User Graph Service page (limit=500), a 900K-follower author requires 1,800 sequential pages ≈ 9–27s of graph reads before any ZADD can complete. Combined with 20K peak post QPS and ~1% near-celebrity authors, dozens of these concurrently block the 500-concurrency worker pool.
bottlenecks.symptom: Kafka consumer lag on `feed.fanout` climbs past 60s, fanout workers appear stuck with high graph-call time in flame graphs, followers of near-celebrity authors wait minutes to see the post while regular-user posts (<500 followers) also get delayed because workers are pinned.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Parallelize graph pagination — request N=10 pages concurrently per author using follower-id hash ranges; cache hot authors' follower lists in a dedicated Redis keyed by author with 30s TTL; lower the celebrity cutoff dynamically to 500K when consumer lag > 30s; offload >100K-follower authors to a separate Kafka topic with a dedicated worker pool tuned for long-running jobs.
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram `fanout_graph_pagination_duration_ms` bucketed by follower_count tier; alert if p99 for 100K–1M tier > 10s. Track `fanout_worker_blocked_on_graph_ratio` — alert at >30%. Correlate with `kafka_consumergroup_lag` on `feed.fanout`.

bottlenecks.title: Redis ZADD pipeline tail latency capping effective fanout throughput
bottlenecks.trigger: Design claims 100 workers × 12K ZADDs/sec = 1.2M writes/sec at peak. But each fanout event triggers 2 ops per follower (ZADD + ZREMRANGEBYRANK), doubling Redis load to ~2.4M ops/sec. Followers are randomly distributed across Redis shards, so a 500-follower pipeline scatter-gathers across ~all shards; one slow shard (GC pause, AOF rewrite) stalls the whole MULTI/EXEC and the worker's 20–100ms service time balloons past 500ms.
bottlenecks.symptom: Per-worker throughput drops from 12K to 2–3K ZADDs/sec during Redis hiccups; total fanout capacity falls below incoming 1.2M/sec demand; consumer lag grows linearly; timeline-cache hit ratio on read side temporarily degrades because recent posts aren't yet written.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Replace MULTI/EXEC with fire-and-forget pipelined commands (no transaction) since ZADDs are independent; shard fanout batches by Redis slot so each pipeline hits exactly one shard; combine ZADD + ZREMRANGEBYRANK into a single Lua script to halve round-trips; add per-shard circuit breaker that sheds load (drops to DLQ for replay) when shard p99 > 50ms; scale workers based on `zadd_latency_p99` not just CPU.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-shard Redis `zadd_latency_ms` p99 (alert >20ms); `fanout_pipeline_scatter_width` histogram (alert if p99 > 50 shards per batch); `fanout_worker_effective_qps` vs configured 12K target — alert at <70% sustained 2 min.

bottlenecks.title: Duplicate-delivery amplification inflating timeline writes under retries
bottlenecks.trigger: Kafka delivery is at-least-once; the worker is idempotent on (follower_id, post_id) but idempotency is enforced at the application layer — duplicate deliveries still execute N redundant ZADDs. During rebalances or broker failover (failureRate 0.0001 but 20K events/sec = 2 events/sec retried, each fanning to 200 followers = 400 extra ZADDs/sec sustained; much higher during actual incidents at 10–50K extra ops/sec).
bottlenecks.symptom: Unexpected Redis write QPS spikes during Kafka consumer rebalances; fanout worker CPU climbs without corresponding increase in fresh post throughput; occasional duplicate ZADD (same score) appears harmless but costs real ops budget; consumer lag recovery after an incident is 2–3x slower than expected.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable Kafka cooperative-sticky rebalancing and raise `session.timeout.ms` to 30s to cut rebalance frequency; commit offsets only after ZADD pipeline success with `enable.auto.commit=false`; add a small in-memory LRU of recently-processed (post_id) keys per worker (~10K entries) to short-circuit obvious duplicates before hitting Redis; use Kafka exactly-once semantics (idempotent producer + transactional consumer) for the Post Service → fanout topic leg.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `fanout_duplicate_event_ratio` = (events_processed - unique_post_ids)/events_processed, alert >1% over 5min; track `kafka_consumer_rebalance_rate` alert >0.1/min; compare `fanout_zadd_count` to expected `post_count × avg_followers` — alert on >5% drift.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Fanout Service exists in this design When someone posts, the Post Service just stores the post and drops an event on Kafka — it doesn't touch any follower's feed. The Fanout Service is the worker that actually *does* the expensive work of updating ~150 follower timelines so that when those followers open the app, their feed is already built. Without this separation, either the poster waits seconds for their post to finish propagating (bad UX), or the feed read path has to do a massive fan-in across every followee's posts on every open (slow feed loads at 100K QPS). The Fanout Service also owns the **celebrity cutoff logic** — the clever hybrid trick where authors with >1M followers *skip* fanout entirely, and their posts get merged in on the read side instead. ## What breaks without it If fanout lived inside the Post Service, a celebrity like an 80M-follower account would trigger 80 million Redis writes on a single POST — the request would time out, the Post Service threads would be pinned for minutes, and regular users trying to post during that window would see 5xx errors. Operators would see Kafka lag climbing, Redis shards hot-spotting on the celebrity's fanout batch, and cascading timeouts back through the Load Balancer. ## The number that matters Peak fanout load is **1.2M timeline writes/sec** (6K posts/sec from non-celebrity authors × ~200 avg followers). Running this as 100 worker replicas × 12K ZADDs/sec each gives headroom. A synchronous path inside Post Service — which only runs at 20K QPS peak — could never absorb a 60× write amplification. ## Trade-off Decoupling means followers see the post 1–5 seconds *after* it's posted, not instantly — eventual consistency in exchange for fast writes and survivable bursts.

sections.heading: Storage
sections.body: Edges sharded in Cassandra keyed by `user_id`, column = `follower_id`. Read-through Redis cache for the hot set.

sections.heading: API
sections.body: `get_followers(user_id, cursor, limit)` returns a page; fanout worker streams all pages.

sections.heading: Celebrity handling
sections.body: For authors above threshold, the service returns early with a flag so the worker skips fanout entirely.

lost: Clustering and sharding are harder than Cassandra at this scale

bottlenecks.title: Follower-list pagination stampede from fanout workers on near-celebrity authors
bottlenecks.trigger: Fanout workers call get_followers(author_id) for every non-celebrity post (6K QPS of posts). Authors with 100K–999K followers (just under the 1M celebrity cutoff) require 200–2000 sequential pages at limit=500 per page. At 20K peak post QPS with even 1% of authors in this tier, that's 200 concurrent paginations × up to 2000 pages = 400K page reads/sec hitting the graph service and its Cassandra backing store on hot author_id partitions.
bottlenecks.symptom: Graph service p99 climbs from ~15ms to 100ms+; a small number of Cassandra nodes owning big-follower-list partitions show 5-10x CPU vs peers; fanout Kafka consumer lag grows because workers are blocked on graph pagination; feed-visibility SLO (1-5s) breaches for followers of popular-but-not-celebrity authors.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cache full follower lists in Redis (`followers:{author_id}`) for authors with >10K followers, TTL 60s, invalidated on follow/unfollow events; serve paginated reads from the cached list rather than Cassandra. For >100K-follower authors, pre-shard the follower list into N=16 Redis keys by hash(follower_id) so fanout workers can parallelize pagination. Bump the celebrity threshold to 500K dynamically when graph p99 > 50ms to shed load onto the read-path.
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram `graph_get_followers_latency_ms` bucketed by author follower_count tier; alert if p99 for 100K-1M tier > 50ms. Per-Cassandra-node CPU variance (max/median > 3x). Track `graph_pagination_pages_per_request` — alert when p99 > 100 pages sustained 2 min.

bottlenecks.title: Hot-partition read amplification on celebrity author_id in Cassandra
bottlenecks.trigger: Edges are sharded keyed by user_id with follower_id as column. A celebrity with 80M followers means one partition holds 80M columns (~2-4 GB per partition), violating Cassandra's recommended <100MB partition size. Even with the celebrity short-circuit flag, any read that touches the partition (moderation scans, analytics, cache rebuild after Redis failover, 'who follows X' product features) hits a single node and its replicas at full force.
bottlenecks.symptom: One Cassandra node pegged at 100% CPU/disk I/O; `nodetool tpstats` shows massive pending ReadStage on celebrity-owning nodes; read timeouts and HintedHandoff backlog; compaction stalls because SSTables for that partition are huge; gossip flaps as the node becomes unresponsive.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Bucket the partition key as `(user_id, bucket_id)` where bucket_id = hash(follower_id) % 32, turning an 80M-row partition into 32 × 2.5M-row partitions spread across the cluster; update get_followers to scatter-gather across buckets in parallel. Return the celebrity-flag directly from a denormalized `user_meta` table (single PK lookup) so the fanout decision never touches the edges table.
bottlenecks.detection: Cassandra partition-size histogram (alert p99 > 100MB); per-node read latency variance; `cassandra_pending_read_stage` > 50 on any single node; track top-N largest partitions weekly and alert on any partition > 500MB.

bottlenecks.title: Graph service outage blocking the entire post write path
bottlenecks.trigger: Post Service calls graph (or relies on denormalized follower_count that graph maintains) to determine the celebrity cutoff on every write. Fanout workers call get_followers on every non-celebrity post. A graph service incident (0.0005 baseline failure × amplified during partial outages) at 20K peak post QPS means posts either fail outright or can't be fanned out — graph becomes a hard dependency for both posting and feed visibility.
bottlenecks.symptom: Spike in Post Service 5xx errors correlated with graph service health; Kafka fanout lag grows because workers retry-loop on graph timeouts; follower-of-outage-author feeds go stale for minutes-to-hours; on-call paged for cascading timeouts through Post Service → fanout worker → graph.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cache `follower_count` denormalized on the user record (`u:{user_id}`) with async updates from a follow-event consumer — eliminates sync graph calls from the post write path entirely. Fanout workers should use circuit breakers (Hystrix/resilience4j) with 500ms timeout and degrade to Kafka retry-with-backoff rather than blocking the worker pool. Keep a stale-but-usable follower-list cache (24h TTL) that the graph can serve from even when Cassandra is degraded.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `post_service_graph_dependency_error_rate` > 0.1%; track `fanout_worker_blocked_on_graph_seconds` — alert at >30s. Dashboard graph service availability correlated with post-write success rate; SLO burn-rate alerts on joint availability.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the User Graph Service is here The news feed design is fundamentally about "show me posts from people I follow" — which means *someone* has to know who follows whom. Every time a user posts, the Fanout Service needs the author's follower list to know whose timeline caches to update. Every time a feed is read, the News Feed Service needs the viewer's celebrity-followee list to do the hybrid merge. That social graph is a separate concern from posts and timelines — it has its own storage pattern (edges, not documents), its own update rate (follow/unfollow events), and its own hot-spot problems (celebrities with tens of millions of inbound edges). Bundling it into the Post Service or a general DB call would mix two very different workloads. ## What happens without it If the Fanout Service queried the primary user DB directly for followers on every post, a single celebrity-adjacent author posting would trigger a multi-page scan against a shared table — blocking unrelated queries. Operators would see Post Service latency spike during viral moments, and a DB incident would take down *both* posting and feed-reading simultaneously because they'd share a failure domain. ## The number that matters At 6K non-celebrity posts/sec, fanout needs follower lists for ~6K authors/sec, each returning up to 1M follower IDs. That's potentially **~1.2M follower-edge reads/sec** (6K posts × 200 avg followers). A dedicated service with its own Redis cache on the hot set and Cassandra shards keyed by `user_id` can absorb that; a general-purpose DB endpoint cannot. ## Trade-off Splitting the graph into its own service adds a network hop on every post write, but gains independent scaling and a clean place to put the celebrity-detection short-circuit.

timeline.name: Timeline Cache (Redis Sorted Sets)
timeline.summary: Per-user precomputed timeline of recent post ids.

sections.heading: Data structure
sections.body: `tl:{user}` = Redis ZSET, score = post timestamp, member = post_id. Bounded to 1000 entries per user.

sections.heading: Capacity
sections.body: 300M users * 1000 * 24B ≈ 7 TB worst case; using 20-item hot caches keeps working set at ~150 GB.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body: - Shard loss loses recent feed slices for affected users. Rebuild by replaying Kafka fanout topic (7d retention) or fan-out-on-read fallback.

sections.heading: Eviction
sections.body: `allkeys-lru`. Inactive users get evicted naturally; they'll fall back to on-read rebuild when they open the app.

gained: Persistent tier + RAM tier in one system
No write amplification — celebrity posts are trivial
lost: Every feed open = N fan-in reads → slow for power users
Hot author posts cause thundering herd on read

bottlenecks.title: Scatter-gather ZADD hotspots from fanout amplification
bottlenecks.trigger: Fanout writes peak at 1.2M ZADDs/sec across ~150 follower timelines per post. Each fanout batch scatters writes across ~all Redis shards (followers are randomly distributed), so a single shard's tail latency (GC, AOF rewrite, slow ZREMRANGEBYRANK on a 1000-entry ZSET) caps the entire pipeline. At 20K peak post QPS × 200 followers × 2 ops (ZADD + ZREMRANGEBYRANK) = 2.4M ops/sec demand.
bottlenecks.symptom: Per-shard Redis CPU variance climbs (max/median > 3x); fanout worker effective throughput drops from target 12K/sec to 2-3K/sec; Kafka fanout consumer lag grows; followers see post-visibility delay grow from ~2s to 30s+; on-call sees one or two Redis shards hot while the cluster looks underutilized in aggregate.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Combine ZADD + ZREMRANGEBYRANK into a single Lua script to halve round-trips; shard fanout batches by Redis hash slot so each pipeline hits one shard; use fire-and-forget pipelining (no MULTI/EXEC) since ZADDs are independent; disable AOF rewrite during peak hours or use `no-appendfsync-on-rewrite yes`; provision cluster for 3x peak ops budget (~7M ops/sec) to absorb tail.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-shard `zadd_latency_ms` p99 (alert >20ms); `redis_shard_cpu_variance` max/median ratio (alert >3x); histogram `timeline_pipeline_duration_ms` p99 (alert >50ms); monitor `redis_commands_processed_total` per shard for skew.

bottlenecks.title: Cold-user miss storm on inactive-return traffic
bottlenecks.trigger: Working set is 150GB (20-post hot cache × 300M users) under `allkeys-lru`. Inactive users (days/weeks away) get evicted. On Monday-morning commute spike or a viral event pulling lapsed users back, 10-20% of 100K feed QPS = 10-20K cold lookups/sec, each triggering on-read rebuild (scan 200 followees' recent posts) or Kafka replay — neither is cheap at sustained rates.
bottlenecks.symptom: Timeline cache hit ratio drops from ~98% to 80-85% after idle periods; feed p95 latency jumps from 30ms to seconds for cold users; News Feed Service thread pools (3000 concurrency) saturate waiting on rebuilds; cascading load on Post Store (Cassandra) and User Graph Service; Kafka replay consumers backlog.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Bump per-user cache from 20 to ~200 post_ids (only ~24B each → ~1.5 TB, still manageable with Redis-on-flash or Aerospike hybrid tier); pre-warm timelines on push-notification-opened signal (login prediction); return a bounded-fanin degraded response (top-10 followees only) with <200ms SLO on cold rebuild; use `volatile-lru` with explicit TTL so eviction is predictable.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert `timeline_cache_hit_ratio < 95%` sustained 2 min; histogram `timeline_cold_rebuild_duration_ms` p99 (alert >500ms); `timeline_cold_rebuild_qps` (alert >2K/sec); track hit ratio by user-activity tier to spot cold-segment regressions.

bottlenecks.title: Shard loss loses recent timeline slices with slow rebuild
bottlenecks.trigger: A Redis shard failure loses the `tl:{user}` ZSETs for the users hashed to it — potentially tens of millions of timelines. Rebuild via Kafka `feed.fanout` replay (7-day retention) is bounded by fanout worker throughput (100 workers × 12K ZADDs/sec = 1.2M/sec), so rebuilding a 1/32 shard's worth of 600M events (20K post QPS × 7 days ÷ 32) ≈ 400M events takes ~5+ minutes even at full capacity, during which affected users get degraded feeds.
bottlenecks.symptom: A chunk of users (~3% per shard in a 32-shard cluster) see empty or truncated feeds immediately post-incident; on-read fallback path spikes, loading Post Store and User Graph; feed p99 for affected users climbs into seconds; Kafka consumer lag spike as replay competes with live fanout traffic.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run Redis in cluster mode with replica-per-shard (`replica-read-only yes`) and automatic failover via Sentinel/Cluster — survives single-node loss without data loss; use separate Kafka consumer group for replay so live fanout isn't starved; prioritize rebuild by user activity (recent-login users first); keep a secondary warm standby tier (Aerospike) that can serve during Redis rebuild.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `redis_cluster_slots_assigned` < full or `redis_connected_slaves < 1` per shard; track `timeline_rebuild_backlog_events` and ETA metric; SLO burn-rate alert on feed p99 > 500ms for >1% of users; synthetic canary that writes/reads from every shard every 30s.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Timeline Cache is here The whole point of this news feed design is that when a user opens the app, they should see their feed *instantly* — no scanning through the posts of 200 followees, no joining tables, no ranking. The Timeline Cache is where that "instant answer" lives: a pre-built list of post IDs for each user, sorted by time, ready to serve. The Fanout Service writes into it whenever someone you follow posts, so by the time you open the app, your feed is already assembled. Without this cache, the News Feed Service would have to compute your feed on every open — scanning 200 followees' recent posts, merging, sorting — against the Post Store. ## What happens without it If the feed were computed on-read from Cassandra, a single feed open becomes ~200 post-range scans. At peak feed load the Post Store would be hammered with hundreds of thousands of scan queries per second, Cassandra's read latency would climb into the hundreds of milliseconds, and users would see multi-second spinners. Operators would see Cassandra CPU pegged and feed p99 falling off a cliff during traffic spikes. ## The number that matters Feed reads peak at **100K QPS**. A Redis ZREVRANGE returns 20 post IDs in ~1ms from memory; a Cassandra fan-in over 200 followees would take ~30-150ms. That's a 30-150× latency improvement, and at 100K QPS it's the difference between ~100 Redis shards and a Cassandra cluster that simply cannot keep up. ## Trade-off The designer accepted ~150 GB of Redis memory and write amplification during fanout in exchange for sub-millisecond feed reads.

postcache.name: Post + User Cache
postcache.summary: Two logical Redis caches the book calls out explicitly for the read path: post cache (post_id → body+meta) and user cache (user_id → display name, avatar, follower count).

sections.heading: Why two caches
sections.body: News feed service fetches 20 post ids, then needs each post's body plus each author's display info. Doing this from the primary DB on every feed GET would be 40 DB hits per feed — Redis collapses that to sub-ms local memory lookups.

sections.heading: Data
Failure modes
sections.body:
- Miss → fall back to DB (3–10ms).
- Stale like_count → acceptable (counters are eventually-consistent; client polls for fresh counts when viewing a post detail).

bottlenecks.title: Hot author key (`u:{celebrity_id}`) saturates a single Redis shard
bottlenecks.trigger: At 100K peak feed QPS, each feed hydrates ~20 posts × ~14 distinct authors = ~1.4M user-key MGETs/sec. When a celebrity (author 101 with 80M followers) is merged in via fan-out-on-read, their `u:101` key is fetched by essentially every viewer who follows them — concentrating 50K–100K GETs/sec on the single hash slot that owns that key, while the cluster average shard sees <5K ops/sec.
bottlenecks.symptom: One Redis shard pegged at 100% CPU while peers are at 20–30%; `u:{celeb}` GET p99 climbs from <1ms to 10–50ms; feed p99 latency spikes during celebrity viral moments; `redis-cli --hotkeys` repeatedly surfaces the same few celeb user ids.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Replicate hot author records into an in-process LRU on each News Feed Service replica with 30–60s TTL (35 replicas × local hit = zero Redis load for celebs); alternatively shard hot keys with a random suffix `u:101:{0..15}` and pick one at read time; pre-identify celebrities via the `celebrity_flag` field and route them through the local cache path.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on per-shard QPS variance (max/median > 3x over 1 min); track `redis_hotkey_qps` per key via `MONITOR` sampling, alert if any single key exceeds 10K GET/sec; dashboard top-20 keys by QPS refreshed every 5 min.

bottlenecks.title: Stale denormalized counters (like_count, follower_count) under 1h TTL
bottlenecks.trigger: `p:{post_id}` caches `like_count` and `comment_count`; `u:{user_id}` caches `follower_count` and `celebrity_flag`. With 1h TTL and write-through on profile updates, a user crossing the 1M-follower celebrity threshold may still be cached as non-celebrity for up to 1h — Post Service keeps fan-out-on-writing for them, creating spurious 1M+ ZADDs per post. Same issue for viral posts where like_count can grow 1000x in minutes but feeds show stale numbers.
bottlenecks.symptom: Fanout Service occasionally processes 1M+ follower fan-outs for an author whose follower count has just crossed the threshold, pinning workers for minutes; users see wildly stale like counts in feed (e.g., '42 likes' on a post actually at 40K); support tickets about 'my feed shows old numbers'.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Split hot counters into a dedicated counter cache with shorter TTL (30s) or use Redis HINCRBY with event-driven invalidation from the likes/follow services via Kafka; for `celebrity_flag` specifically, maintain an in-memory bloom/set of known celebrity IDs refreshed every 5 min so the threshold decision doesn't depend on `u:{user_id}` freshness.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `cache_staleness_seconds` measured by comparing cached counter vs DB counter on a 1% sample; alert if p99 staleness > 120s; track `celebrity_threshold_misclassification_count` by comparing fanout decision vs current follower_count — alert on any occurrence.

bottlenecks.title: Cache stampede on viral-post expiry triggers DB thundering herd
bottlenecks.trigger: A viral post appearing in millions of feeds (via celeb merge) has its `p:{post_id}` key TTL expire after 1h. At 100K feed QPS, the instant that key expires, potentially thousands of concurrent News Feed Service requests all miss simultaneously and fall through to Post Store (Cassandra, 3–10ms). That's a sudden burst of 5K–20K identical SELECTs for one post_id hitting a single Cassandra partition.
bottlenecks.symptom: Periodic 100ms+ latency spikes at TTL boundaries; Cassandra read QPS on single partitions spikes to tens of thousands briefly; feed p99 sawtooth pattern correlated with top-post TTL expiries; `post_cache_miss_ratio` briefly spikes from baseline 0.5% to 5%+.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use probabilistic early expiration (XFetch algorithm) so popular keys refresh ~30s before TTL rather than all at once; add request coalescing / singleflight in the News Feed Service so concurrent misses for the same post_id trigger only one DB read; extend TTL to 24h for posts <7 days old (the hot window) since post bodies are immutable; on miss, use `SET NX` with a short lock key to serialize rebuild.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `post_cache_miss_rate` in 1s buckets, alert on spikes >3x baseline; monitor Cassandra `read_qps_per_partition` p99, alert if any single partition exceeds 1K QPS sustained 10s; log `singleflight_coalesced_count` to measure stampede suppression effectiveness.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Post + User Cache is here The Timeline Cache only stores *post IDs* — a compact list like `[9412300871, 9412300854,...]`. That's useless to the user: they need to see the actual post body, the author's name and avatar, the like count. Someone has to turn those 20 IDs into 20 fully-rendered posts on every single feed open. If the News Feed Service went to Cassandra for this every time, each feed request would cost ~20 post lookups plus ~14 author lookups (some posts share authors) — roughly **34 DB hits per feed page**. The Post + User Cache exists so those 34 lookups become Redis MGETs that return in ~1ms from memory instead of 3–10ms from Cassandra. ## What happens without it Remove this cache and every feed open slams the Post Store and User DB directly. Users see feeds load in 300–800ms instead of 30–80ms — noticeably laggy scrolling. Operators watch Cassandra CPU climb toward 100%, read latency p99 spikes, and — worst — the Post Store's write path (which is handling 20K post writes/sec at peak) starts competing with the read storm and **post submissions start timing out**. A read-path problem becomes a write-path outage. ## The number that matters Feed reads peak at **100K QPS**. At 34 hydration lookups per feed, that's **3.4M key lookups/sec**. Redis handles that comfortably across a modest cluster; Cassandra at 3–10ms per lookup would need hundreds of nodes just to serve reads, on top of the write cluster. ## Trade-off The designer accepted stale counters (like_count can lag by up to an hour under the 1h TTL) in exchange for sub-millisecond hydration.

notif.name: Notification Service
notif.summary: Sends a push/email 'X posted' ping to followers who opted in. Called by the post service (or the fanout service) on new post creation.

sections.heading: Why this is in the news-feed design
sections.body: The book's final diagram includes a notification service next to the fanout service — posting is usually paired with an out-of-app ping (esp. for close friends or celebrity posts). Decoupling it from fanout means notification throttling / quiet-hours are handled by the dedicated notif system (see ).

sections.heading: Integration
sections.body: Post service produces a 'new_post' event to a Kafka topic; the notif service consumes, resolves close-friends / celebrity-followers for the author, dedupes per (viewer, author, day), and sends a push with a deep link to the post.

sections.heading: Throttling
sections.body: Celebrity accounts with millions of followers don't send a push to everyone — only subscribers who explicitly turned on post-notifications for that account (opt-in). Otherwise the notification system would DoS user lock-screens.

bottlenecks.title: Celebrity push-notification fan-out amplification
bottlenecks.trigger: A celebrity (>1M followers) posts and the notification service must resolve opted-in subscribers and emit pushes. Even with opt-in throttling, a top account with 80M followers and just 5% opt-in = 4M pushes per post. At peak posting (20K posts/sec) with ~20% from celebrities = 4K celeb posts/sec; a single A-list post can dwarf the baseline 7K posts/sec in notification volume within seconds.
bottlenecks.symptom: Kafka `feed.notif` consumer lag climbs past minutes; APNs/FCM provider rate limits return 429s; push delivery p99 stretches from seconds to 10+ minutes; users report 'notification arrived hours after the post'; on-call sees notif worker CPU pinned and downstream provider error rate spiking.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Maintain an explicit `post_notif_subscribers:{author_id}` Redis SET populated on opt-in (not a scan of all followers); shard delivery across a dedicated worker pool with per-provider (APNs/FCM) rate-limit-aware token buckets; for >1M-subscriber authors, parallelize via a second Kafka topic `feed.notif.celeb` with 500+ partitions keyed by subscriber_id; cap per-author push rate to protect lock-screens.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `notif_consumer_lag_seconds > 60`; track `notif_fanout_size` histogram bucketed by author tier, alert when p99 >100K; monitor APNs/FCM `provider_429_rate` and `push_delivery_latency_ms` p99 with alert at >30s.

bottlenecks.title: Dedupe key explosion from per-(viewer, author, day) tracking
bottlenecks.trigger: Dedupe key is (viewer, author, day). At 300M DAU each following ~200 accounts, the theoretical dedupe key space per day is 60B entries — in practice bounded by actual posts, but at 7K posts/sec × avg 150 opted-in subscribers ≈ 1M dedupe checks/sec and ~90B entries/day if even a fraction of follower-author pairs see activity. At ~60B with 50B avg per entry = multi-TB Redis footprint daily.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis memory pressure triggers eviction of dedupe keys mid-day → users receive duplicate pushes ('X posted' twice in one day); Redis OOM alerts; dedupe check latency climbs from <1ms to 10ms+ under memory pressure; support tickets about notification spam.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use `SET dedup:{viewer}:{author}:{yyyymmdd} 1 EX 86400 NX` with `volatile-ttl` eviction instead of unbounded sets; alternatively use a per-viewer daily Bloom filter (`bloom:{viewer}:{yyyymmdd}`, ~1KB each, 300M × 1KB = 300GB manageable) trading a small false-positive rate (missed pushes) for bounded memory; shard dedupe Redis cluster separately from other caches.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on dedupe Redis `used_memory_percent > 80%`; track `duplicate_push_sent_count` derived from client-side receipts, alert if >0.1% of pushes; monitor `dedupe_check_latency_ms` p99 with alert at 5ms.

bottlenecks.title: Kafka `feed.notif` ordering and retry cascade on provider outages
bottlenecks.trigger: APNs or FCM regional outages (happens a few times/year) cause push sends to fail. With at-least-once Kafka delivery and ~7K posts/sec steady-state generating ~1M push attempts/sec to opted-in followers, a 5-minute provider outage backs up 300M push attempts. Naive retry-in-place blocks the consumer offset; naive commit-and-retry loses pushes.
bottlenecks.symptom: Notif consumer lag grows at 1M msgs/sec during provider incidents; after recovery, a thundering herd of retried pushes arrives simultaneously — users get a burst of stale 'X posted' notifications for hours-old posts; Kafka broker disk fills from 7-day retention of backed-up notif events.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Implement a dead-letter topic `feed.notif.retry` with exponential backoff (1m, 5m, 30m) and a max-age filter that drops pushes older than 1h (stale notifications are worse than missed ones); circuit-break per-provider and per-region, shedding to the retry topic when provider error rate >5%; use separate consumer groups per provider so an APNs outage doesn't block FCM deliveries.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `notif_provider_error_rate > 1%` per provider; track `notif_push_age_at_send_ms` p99, alert if >5min (indicates stale delivery); monitor `feed.notif.retry` queue depth with alert at >1M messages; SLO burn-rate alert on end-to-end post-to-push latency.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Notification Service is here In a news feed, seeing a post *when you open the app* is only half the product — the other half is the push notification that pulls you back in ("Jamie just posted"). For 300M DAU, those pings are what drives return visits. But sending a push is a totally different job than updating a timeline cache: it talks to external providers (APNs for iOS, FCM for Android), it has per-user quiet hours, it needs opt-in lists, and it must dedupe so you don't get buzzed twice for the same post. Mixing that logic into the Post Service or the Fanout Service would tangle two unrelated failure domains. ## What breaks without it Imagine push logic lives inside the Fanout Service. A celebrity posts, fanout tries to deliver 80M pushes, APNs starts returning 429s, and suddenly the fanout workers — whose real job is writing to follower timeline caches — are stuck in retry loops against Apple's servers. Operators see Kafka fanout lag climb, regular users' feeds stop updating, and the post-visibility SLO breaches for everyone. A notification-provider outage becomes a feed outage. ## The number that matters At **7K posts/sec sustained**, if each post pings even ~150 opted-in followers, that's ~1M push attempts/sec. A celebrity post at 5% opt-in on 80M followers = 4M pushes from a *single* event. That workload needs its own service with its own rate-limit-aware worker pool — you can't bolt it onto the write path. ## Trade-off Decoupling adds another Kafka topic and another consumer to operate, in exchange for isolating provider outages from the core feed pipeline.

operations.title: Create a post (regular user — fan-out-on-write)
operations.name: Create a post (regular user — fan-out-on-write)
operations.description: POST /posts — post service writes to Post Store, enqueues fanout + notification. Fanout service asynchronously prepends the post_id into each follower's news-feed cache.

steps.title: User taps 'Post'
steps.action: Client POSTs the draft with an idempotency key and optimistic UI (post appears immediately in the composer user's own feed).
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST /posts HTTP/1.1
Idempotency-Key: post-draft-481723
Content-Type: application/json { "body": "Visiting Kyoto! ", "media_refs": ["s3://media/kyoto-cherry.jpg"]
}

steps.title: Load balancer routes to post service
steps.action: L7 LB forwards to a healthy post service replica. Consistent-hash on user_id keeps a single user's writes on the same replica for better cache locality.

steps.title: Post service validates + dedupes
steps.action: Checks idempotency key, validates length (<= 5K chars), resolves media refs, assigns a snowflake post_id.
steps.codeOrCommand:
if redis.sismember('idemp:4782', 'post-draft-481723'): return 200, existing_post_id
pid = snowflake.next
post = Post(pid, user_id=4782, body=body, created_at=now, media=media_refs)

steps.title: Post persisted to source of truth
steps.action: Single-row INSERT into `posts` table. LOCAL_QUORUM for durability. Author's follower_count (150) is attached so the fanout service can decide write-vs-read without an extra lookup.

steps.title: Fanout event enqueued (parallel with notification)
steps.action: Post service produces to `feed.fanout` with key=author_id. At-least-once; fanout service is idempotent on (follower_id, post_id).

steps.title: Notification event emitted (parallel)
steps.action: A 'new_post' event is also emitted for the notification service so followers with post-notifications opted-in get a push.

steps.title: Post service returns 201 immediately
steps.action: Fanout is NOT awaited — 201 ships as soon as the DB ack + queue ack return. End-to-end write latency ~20–40ms.

steps.title: LB returns to client
steps.action: Return path through the LB.

steps.title: UI reconciles optimistic state
steps.action: Client swaps the optimistic post with the server-assigned post_id. Followers' feeds will show the post within 1–5 seconds once fanout completes.

operations.title: Fanout on write (regular user, 150 followers)
operations.name: Fanout on write (regular user, 150 followers)
operations.description: Async: fanout service reads the event, pages through followers, and ZADDs into each follower's news-feed cache. Book's default path for non-celebrity users.

steps.title: Fanout service polls the topic
steps.action: A fanout-service consumer in group 'fanout-prod' fetches a batch of records. The record for post 9412300871 is ready.

steps.title: Fanout service decides: write-path
steps.action: follower_count = 150 is well below the 1M celebrity threshold → do fan-out-on-write. Proceed to load the follower list from the user graph.
steps.codeOrCommand:
if event.follower_count > 1_000_000: return # celebrity — handled by fan-out-on-read
# else: normal fan-out-on-write path

steps.title: User graph returns 150 followers
steps.action: Single read from the follower-edges table. Small enough to fit in one response page.
steps.codeOrCommand: SELECT follower_id FROM followers WHERE user_id=4782 LIMIT 500;

steps.title: Fanout service ZADDs post_id to 150 news-feed caches
