steps.action: Pipelined Redis writes — 150 ZADDs in a single Redis MULTI/EXEC. Each follower's timeline ZSET gets the post_id with score=created_at; old entries beyond 1000 are trimmed.

operations.title: Celebrity posts (fan-out-on-READ path)
operations.name: Celebrity posts (fan-out-on-READ path)
operations.description: A celebrity with 80M followers posts. Fanout service skips the write; at read time, the news feed service merges the celebrity's posts from a dedicated celeb-posts sorted set. Book's hybrid solution to the write-amplification problem.

steps.title: Fanout event for celebrity author
steps.action: A record for author 101 (80M followers) lands in the fanout queue.

steps.title: Fanout service: skip the write
steps.action: follower_count > 1M → do NOT fan-out-on-write. Instead write the post_id to a celebrity-posts ZSET keyed by the author (single write vs 80M writes). Feed reads will merge this in at read time.
steps.codeOrCommand: if event.follower_count > 1_000_000: redis.zadd(f'celeb-posts:{event.author_id}', {event.post_id: event.created_at.timestamp}) return # do NOT populate 80M timelines

steps.title: Single write to celeb-posts cache
steps.action: One Redis write — O(1) — replaces what would have been 80M writes. This is the book's central efficiency argument for the hybrid model.
steps.note: The write amplification savings here (80M → 1) are why Twitter / Instagram / Facebook all use a hybrid approach.

operations.title: Load feed page (hybrid read)
operations.name: Load feed page (hybrid read)
operations.description: GET /feed — news feed service reads the precomputed timeline, merges any celebrity posts, and hydrates post + author details from caches.

steps.title: User opens the app
steps.action: Client requests the first page of the feed with a null cursor.

steps.title: LB routes to news feed service
steps.action: Consistent-hash on user_id routes to a feed service replica with warm cache affinity for this user's timeline shard.

steps.title: News feed service reads the precomputed timeline
steps.action: Issue `ZREVRANGE tl:4782 0 19 WITHSCORES` to fetch the top 20 post_ids. Also load the user's list of followed celebrities from cache.
steps.codeOrCommand:
tl_ids = redis.zrevrange(f'tl:{user_id}', 0, 19, withscores=True)
celebs = cache.get(f'celebs_followed:{user_id}') or graph.celebs_followed(user_id)
# celebs = [101, 202] (user follows 2 celebrities)

steps.title: News feed cache returns top-20 post ids (regular) + celeb posts
steps.action: Redis returns 20 ids in sub-ms. Then another ZREVRANGE for each celeb the user follows returns their recent posts (typically <10 each).
steps.codeOrCommand:
ZREVRANGE tl:4782 0 19 WITHSCORES
# 20 (post_id, score) pairs from precomputed feed
ZREVRANGE celeb-posts:101 0 9 WITHSCORES
ZREVRANGE celeb-posts:202 0 9 WITHSCORES
# merge by score, keep top 20 overall

steps.title: Hydrate post bodies + author display from caches
steps.action: Batch MGET on `p:{post_id}` for 20 posts and `u:{author_id}` for the distinct authors. The book calls these out as the post cache and user cache — critical to keeping feed latency under 50ms.

steps.title: Fallback DB read for cache misses
steps.action: Of the 20 posts, 2 missed the post cache (older content evicted from LRU). News feed service fetches them from the posts table and backfills the cache asynchronously.
steps.codeOrCommand:
SELECT post_id, author_id, body, media_refs FROM posts
WHERE post_id IN ('8201...', '8202...');

steps.title: Assemble response
steps.action: Compose the 20 hydrated posts + pagination cursor. The cursor encodes the min score seen so the next page continues after this timestamp.

steps.title: LB streams response back
steps.action: Return path.

steps.title: Feed renders
steps.action: Client renders 20 posts. End-to-end p95 around 30–80ms with warm caches. First-scroll perceived latency is minimal because the client prefetches media thumbnails in parallel.

tradeoffs.chosen: Hybrid push for regular users, pull for celebrities
tradeoffs.rationale: Pure push breaks on 100M-follower posts; pure pull makes every feed GET fan in across thousands of authors. The hybrid localizes the hot path while keeping most reads cheap. Cost: two code paths and a tunable threshold.

tradeoffs.chosen: Redis LIST per user, capped at 1000
tradeoffs.rationale: Fixed memory per user (300M users * 1000 post_ids * 24B ≈ 7 TB), O(1) prepend, O(N) range for pagination. Losing entries beyond the cap means deep scrolling falls back to DB, which is an acceptable tail.
Offset pagination gets unstable when new posts arrive between pages. A monotonic cursor gives stable, deep pagination and plays well with Redis LRANGE and DB range scans.

tradeoffs.chosen: 202 accepted after Kafka enqueue, not after fanout
tradeoffs.rationale: Fanout can take seconds for a large follower list; blocking the user on it would make posting feel slow. The cost is that a follower can refresh faster than the worker propagates — optimistic UI on the author hides it.

tradeoffs.chosen: Sharded relational DB keyed by author_id
tradeoffs.rationale: Posts are mostly read by (author_id, time) for the pull path and by post_id for hydration — both served well by a relational shard. Co-locating an author's posts keeps celebrity pull-reads on one shard.

Handle unfollow — lazy cleanup vs immediate invalidation of the timeline cache
Design a realtime 'new posts available' banner without polling
Extend for stories (24h TTL) and reels (vertical video) on the same feed
Cross-region replication so a feed read in EU does not cross the Atlantic
